title: 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy
author: Hamilton Helmer
thesisParagraph: 7 Powers teaches that durable strategy is not a list of goals, a better product, or operational competence. A business has Power only when it has both a benefit that improves economics or willingness to pay and a barrier that keeps competitors from arbitraging that benefit away. The seven forms are scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, and process power. The reader learns to test each claimed advantage by asking what benefit it creates, what barrier protects it, and whether the timing of the market allows that power to form.

coreIdeas.name: Benefit plus barrier
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A strategic advantage matters only when it improves economics and blocks rivals from copying away the gain.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: force every claimed advantage to name its benefit and its barrier

coreIdeas.name: Seven distinct powers
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Each power works through a different mechanism, so loose moat language hides the real test.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: classify the advantage by mechanism before deciding what to build

coreIdeas.name: Timing shapes possibility
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Some powers can form only during origination, take-off, or stability, and missed windows cannot be wished back open.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: match the power to the stage where it can realistically emerge

coreIdeas.name: Operational excellence is not enough
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Better execution can help a business but it does not become strategy until it creates a protected advantage.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: separate copyable improvement from barrier-forming invention or process

coreIdeas.name: Do not worship size or novelty
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Growth, users, invention, patents, and reputation are raw materials, not Power, until their protection logic is visible.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: test the exact condition that turns a common business asset into durable power

targetReader: Founders, operators, investors, product leaders, and managers who need to tell the difference between a business that merely performs well today and a business protected against future competition. They care because capital, hiring, and product choices change once the actual source of power is named.

signatureMoves: uses strategy capital, power types, and benefit-barrier logic
keeps examples tied to durable differential returns
forces every advantage claim through a barrier test
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not call scale or brand a power without the barrier.
Do not make strategy sound like ordinary competitiveness.

voiceAntiSpecimens: In this chapter, readers will learn about the importance of strategic moats.
Businesses should leverage innovation to maximize sustainable competitive advantage.
The key takeaway is that strong companies are better positioned to win over time.
Try to be intentional about creating value and staying ahead of competitors.
Power is a journey of discovering your unique business strengths.
teachingArc: The first seven chapters teach each power as a separate mechanism, moving from cost and user-value advantages through incumbent traps, customer lock-in, trust premiums, scarce inputs, and embedded processes. The final two chapters turn the list into judgment: first by showing that power must be invented or chosen rather than optimized into existence, then by matching each power to the stage where it can still form.
forbiddenMoves: Do not turn every chapter into generic moat language; each power needs its own benefit, barrier, and failure test.
Do not treat operational excellence, growth, user count, branding, or patents as Power without proving the protective mechanism.
Do not invent detailed company case histories beyond Netflix, Intel, Facebook, and LinkedIn as supported in the sidecars.
Do not let examples collapse into boardroom decks, generic startups, classrooms, kitchens, or repeated spreadsheet scenes.
Do not discuss power without benefit and barrier.
Do not soften Helmer into generic strategy advice.
